title: Weston v. Cassata (2001)
summary: A statute's statement that welfare benefits are not an entitlement does not strip due process protection from recipients when the rest of the scheme gives officials no discretion to withhold benefits from eligible participants, so defective sanction notices violated due process.
notes:
Key line: "Despite the state officials' active role in distributing welfare monies, that role has no discretionary component beyond the authority to withhold or distribute benefits according to statute." (Davidson, J.)

Citation: 37 P.3d 469 (Colo. App. 2001).

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were Frances F. Weston, Christine M. Kneubehl and Shauna Parks, later known as Shauna Disher, suing on behalf of themselves and a class of all recipients of welfare benefits in Adams County, Colorado, who had been sent sanction notices. The defendants on appeal were Donald M. Cassata, Director of the Adams County Department of Social Services, sued in his official capacity, and the Adams County Board of Social Services. The Denver Department of Social Services and its manager settled before trial, and the Colorado Department of Human Services and its executive director were not parties to the appeal.
sections.Material Facts: The federal welfare reform act of 1996 replaced Aid to Families with Dependent Children with Temporary Assistance to Needy Families, and declared that it should not be interpreted to entitle any individual to assistance. Colorado's 1997 Colorado Works Program Act also disclaimed any legal entitlement but provided that, subject to available appropriations, a participant shall receive a basic assistance grant and shall continue to receive it during an appeal. Counties sanctioned noncompliance by reducing cash assistance, after a notice that state regulations required to describe the action, its reason, amount and effective date, and the right to a county conference and state appeal. Between July 1997 and November 1999 Adams County used five versions of sanction notices. None stated the amount of the sanction or a specific reason, and early versions gave twenty six rather than ninety days to appeal. The county routinely reinstated benefits to anyone who appealed but kept using the defective forms.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs brought a class action in state district court under the Uniform Declaratory Judgments Law, the Colorado Administrative Procedure Act and 42 U.S.C. section 1983, seeking a declaration that the notices were inadequate, an injunction, reversal of sanctions, restitution of withheld benefits, and attorney fees. After a bench trial the court found that none of the five versions of the notices met statutory or regulatory requirements and that the defendants had violated due process under the state and federal constitutions; it declared the notices inadequate, enjoined their use, ordered the sanction records removed, and ordered restoration of withheld benefits. The defendants appealed to the Colorado Court of Appeals, Division I, which affirmed on July 5, 2001, in an opinion by Judge Davidson joined by Judges Metzger and Roy. The Colorado Supreme Court denied certiorari on January 14, 2002.
sections.Issue: Whether the county and its director were persons subject to suit under section 1983; whether TANF recipients retained a property interest in continued welfare benefits protected by the Due Process Clause after Congress and the Colorado General Assembly declared that the programs created no entitlement; whether the Adams County sanction notices, which omitted the amount and specific reason for the sanction and misstated the appeal period, satisfied due process; and whether the plaintiffs' failure to exhaust individual administrative appeals deprived the trial court of jurisdiction over their state law claims.
sections.Holding: The court affirmed on every point. County agencies and officers responsible for implementing a state statute are persons under section 1983 in an action for prospective relief. Despite the no entitlement language, recipients who have met the statutory standards and begun receiving benefits hold a property right, although not an unlimited one, because officials have no discretion to withhold benefits from eligible participants when funds have been allocated. Notices that failed to comply with the state regulation setting minimum notice requirements deprived the plaintiffs of due process. Exhaustion was not required because the county's practice of reinstating benefits to everyone who appealed made further administrative review futile and prevented the notice problem from ever reaching judicial review.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Davidson explained that under Board of Regents v. Roth a property interest exists when rules or understandings secure a benefit and support a legitimate claim of entitlement, and that the degree of discretion left to the decisionmaker is the key. Reading the welfare statutes as a whole, the court concluded that the no entitlement language removed the absolute entitlement of the AFDC era and addressed the contingency of federal block grant funding, but did not erase every form of entitlement. Once a state has received a block grant and a participant meets the statutory criteria, the county acts only as a conduit, and state and county officials conceded at trial that eligible participants must be paid when funds are available. The court drew on Washington Legal Clinic for the Homeless v. Barry for the proposition that the less discretion an official has, the more likely a benefit is property, and for its doubt that blanket disclaimers can strip entitlements conferred by unequivocal statutes. It relied on Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill for the rule that a legislature may not authorize deprivation of a conferred property interest without procedural safeguards. Because a state regulation set the minimum content of a sanction notice, that regulation defined the minimum process due, and notices omitting the sanction amount, a specific reason, or the correct appeal period were inadequate as a matter of law.

topics.lrs-o-new-property: Mandatory state benefit and appeal provisions constrained discretion sufficiently to create the interest despite general federal no-entitlement language.
topics.lrs-o-due-process-framework: The protected-interest question in Weston is the first step of the procedural due process framework.

learning.separateOpinions: None. Judges Metzger and Roy concurred in Judge Davidson's opinion for a unanimous division.
